You pass if both versions are written, the swap in the long constructor is real, meaning two same-typed arguments actually exchanged, and the designated initialiser is shown free of that risk. A builder earns its place once the configuration also needs a rule a single struct cannot check by itself, such as one field's valid range depending on another's, which the exercise below is about; for four independent fields with no such rule, the designated initialiser is already the whole answer.

Builder separates constructing a complex object from the object itself: instead of one constructor that takes every field, a separate class collects the values, usually through chained methods that each return the builder, and produces the finished object from a final
. The class being built is the
; the class collecting the values is the

The problem is a constructor with many parameters, some required and some optional, where positional arguments of the same type can be swapped without the compiler noticing, and every optional combination that used to need its own overload now needs none, because the builder's methods are named and called in any order. Before named arguments existed in the language, this was the only way to give a constructor call readable names.
The mechanism, in modern C++, mostly already exists without writing a builder at all: a struct with a designated initialiser gives every field a name at the call site,

, in less code than a builder class and with the same protection against a positional swap. What a plain struct cannot do is check a rule that spans several fields, or reject a value that is individually well-typed but out of range; a designated initialiser sets whatever is written and defaults whatever is not, with no step where "is this any good" gets asked.
What a builder costs, beyond the struct it usually wraps, is one class whose only job is calling that struct's own validation from

; the validation does the real work, and the builder is a name for the shape a caller writes it in. Where the validation is the point, a validating factory function does the same check with no class at all:
returning the checked type, or throwing.

You meet this wherever a configuration has fields that must be filled in before it means anything, and the interview question is exactly the boundary: a designated initialiser for values that only need naming, a validating factory or a builder for values that also need checking.

subs.title: Builder versus long constructors versus designated initialisers

c.v: The classic Builder wraps the same struct the cold check already had, one method per optional field, each returning the builder so calls can be chained:

blocks.text:

designated: kp 2.5, ki 0.1, kd 0.05, limit 100
same values: true

c.v: produce the same object, and the second one needed no class. Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides describe Builder in the creational chapter of the 1994 catalogue (

) as separating the construction of a complex object from its representation, written for a language whose constructors take positional arguments and cannot check anything about them individually as they are set. C++20's designated initialiser reaches most of the same goal, named values at the call site, in a language where it was never true that a struct could only be filled in positionally, and Core Guidelines
has asked all along for a call that says what it means, which a designated initialiser now gives you directly.
What a designated initialiser cannot do is refuse a value. It sets

to whatever is written, checks nothing about it, and defaults every field left out, which is exactly as far as a plain struct goes: naming values, not judging them. That gap, not the four fields themselves, is where a builder, or something smaller, still earns a place, and the worked example measures exactly where the line falls.
A field that is left out of a designated initialiser is one question a struct still answers for you, as long as that field has no default of its own:
